{{Short description|Traditional English song}}
{{Use British English|date=October 2013}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=October 2020}}
"'''Scarborough Fair'''" ({{English folk song|roud=12|child=2}}) is a traditional Northern English [[ballad]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://mainlynorfolk.info/martin.carthy/songs/scarboroughfair.html |title=The Elfin Knight / Scarborough Fair / Whittingham Fair|website=mainlynorfolk.info|access-date=2020-05-07}}</ref> The song lists a number of [[adynaton|impossible tasks]] given to a former lover who lives in [[Scarborough, North Yorkshire]]. The "Scarborough/Whittingham Fair" variant was most common in [[Yorkshire]] and [[Northumbria (modern)|Northumbria]], where it was sung to various melodies, often using [[Dorian mode]], with refrains resembling "parsley, sage, rosemary and thyme" and "Then she'll be a true love of mine."<ref>{{Cite web|title=Search: Scarborough Fair RN12|url=https://www.vwml.org/search?q=scarborough%20fair%20rn12&is=1|website=[[Vaughan Williams Memorial Library]]}}</ref> A version appears in ''Traditional Tunes'' (1891) by [[Frank Kidson]], who claims to have collected it from [[Whitby]].<ref name="Kidson">{{cite book |last=Kidson |first=Frank|author-link=Frank Kidson|chapter=Scarborough Fair|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/imslp-tunes-kidson-frank/page/42/mode/2up|title=Traditional Tunes|publisher=Chas. Taphouse & Son |publication-place=Oxford |date=1891 |oclc=47625906 |pages=42–44 |hdl=2027/umn.31951001728562y?urlappend=%3Bseq=45}} Republished in 1999: {{ISBN|9781861430816}}</ref>

The melody best known today was collected from Mark Anderson (1874–1953), a retired lead miner from [[Middleton-in-Teesdale]], [[County Durham]], England, by [[Ewan MacColl]] in 1947. This version was recorded by a number of musicians in the 20th century, including the 1966 arrangement in [[counterpoint]] by the American [[folk rock]] duo [[Simon & Garfunkel]], who learned the ballad from [[Martin Carthy]]. A slightly different rendition of the ballad (referred to as "The Cambric Shirt", or "Parsley, Sage, Rosemary and Thyme") had been recorded by [[John Lomax]] in 1939 in the United States. [[Sarah Brightman]] also performed it as part of her album ''[[La Luna (Sarah Brightman album)|La Luna]]'' from the year 2000.

==History==
The lyrics of "Scarborough Fair" appear to have something in common with a Scottish ballad titled "[[The Elfin Knight]]",<ref name="Kidson" /> collected by [[Francis James Child]] as [[Child Ballad]] #2,<ref>{{cite book |last=Child |first=Francis James |author-link=Francis James Child |title=The English and Scottish Popular Ballads, Part 9 |publisher=[[Houghton Mifflin Harcourt]]|location=Boston / Cambridge |year=1894 |volume=9 |page=206 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xNMVAAAAYAAJ}}</ref> which has been traced as far back as 1670. In this ballad, an [[elf]] threatens to abduct a young woman to be his lover unless she can perform an impossible task ("For thou must shape a [[wikt:sark|sark]] to me / Without any cut or heme, quoth he"); she responds with a list of tasks that he must first perform ("I have an [[acre|aiker]] of good ley-land / Which lyeth low by yon sea-strand").

Dozens of versions existed by the end of the 18th century. A number of older versions refer to locations other than Scarborough Fair, including Wittingham Fair, Cape Ann, "twixt Berwik and Lyne", etc. Many versions do not mention a place name and are often generically titled ("The Lovers' Tasks", "My Father Gave Me an Acre of Land", etc.).{{citation needed|date=October 2021}}

The references to the traditional English gathering "[[Scarborough Fair (fair)|Scarborough Fair]]", and the refrain "[[parsley]], [[salvia officinalis|sage]], [[rosemary]], and [[thyme]]", date to 19th-century versions, and may have been borrowed from the ballad ''[[Riddles Wisely Expounded]]'' ([[Child Ballad]] #1), which has a similar plot.{{citation needed|date=October 2021}}

The lyrics published by Frank Kidson in 1891<ref name="Kidson" /> represent the most widely recognized version of the song. However, subsequent performers have frequently selected and rearranged verses. Martin Carthy, for example, replaced the final verse with a repetition of the opening stanza, while Simon and Garfunkel recorded a sequence consisting of verses 1, 2, 5, and 7, concluding with a reprise of the first verse. This latter arrangement has been widely adopted by later artists. The following are the lyrics as published by Kidson:
<poem>{{0|—}}''The male:''
O, where are you going? To Scarborough Fair?
Savoury, sage, rosemary and thyme,
Remember me to a lass that lives there,
For she was once a true love of mine.

And tell her to make me a cambric shirt,
Savoury, sage, rosemary and thyme,
Without any seam or needlework,
And then she shall be a true love of mine.

And tell her to wash it in yonder dry well,
Savoury, sage, rosemary and thyme,
Where no water sprung nor a drop of rain fell,
And then she shall be a true love of mine.

And tell her to dry it on yonder thorn,
Savoury, sage, rosemary and thyme,
Which never bore blossom since Adam was born,
And then she shall be a true love of mine.

{{0|—}}''The female:''
O, will you find me an acre of land,
Savoury, sage, rosemary and thyme,
Between the sea foam and the sea sand,
Or never you'll be a true love of mine.

O, will you plough it with a ram's horn,
Savoury, sage, rosemary and thyme,
And sow it all over with one peppercorn,
Or else you'll be a true love of mine.

Or will you reap it with a sickle of leather,
Savoury, sage, rosemary and thyme,
And tie it all up with a peacock's feather,
Or never you'll be a true love of mine.

And when you have done and have finished your work,
Savoury, sage, rosemary and thyme,
You can come to me for your cambric shirt,
And then you shall be a true love of mine.</poem>

===Alternative refrains===
The oldest versions of "[[The Elfin Knight]]" (circa 1650) contain the refrain "my plaid away, my plaid away, the wind shall not blow my plaid away." Slightly more recent versions often contain one of a group of related refrains:
*"Sober and grave grows merry in time"
*"Every rose grows merry with time"
*"There's never a rose grows fairer with time"
*"Whilst every grove rings with a merry antine"{{efn|1=For "antine", see the French word {{lang|fr|[[wikt:antienne#French|antienne]]}} ('chant' or 'refrain').}}<ref>{{cite book|first=Sabine|last=Baring-Gould|author-link=Sabine Baring-Gould|chapter=Riddles|title=Strange Survivals|year=1892|publisher=Methuen & Co.|publication-place=London|page=226|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/strangesurvivals00bari/page/226}}</ref>

These are usually paired with "Once (s)he was a true love of mine" or some variant. "Parsley, sage, rosemary and thyme" may simply be an alternate rhyming refrain to the original based on a corruption of "grows merry in time" into "rosemary and thyme".{{citation needed|reason=OR|date=October 2020}}

===Anderson melody===

The version of the melody best-known today was sung to [[Ewan MacColl]] in 1947 by Mark Anderson (1874–1953), a retired lead miner from [[Middleton-in-Teesdale]], [[County Durham]], England.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Famous song has roots in Dale folk|url=https://www.thenorthernecho.co.uk/news/9400217.famous-song-roots-dale-folk/|access-date=2020-08-29|newspaper=[[The Northern Echo]]|date=3 December 2011 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Scarborough Fair (Roud Folksong Index S160453)|url=https://www.vwml.org/record/RoudFS/S160453|access-date=2020-08-29|website=[[Vaughan Williams Memorial Library]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Harvey |first=Todd|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m9MHAQAAMAAJ&q=scarborough+fair+mark+anderson|title=The Formative Dylan: Transmission and Stylistic Influences, 1961–1963|date=2001|publisher=Scarecrow Press|isbn=978-0-8108-4115-4|pages=33|language=en}}</ref> No audio recording of Anderson's version was ever made, although [[Alan Lomax]] recorded Anderson singing other songs in 1951.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mark Anderson |url=https://archive.culturalequity.org/person/anderson-mark |access-date=2022-07-12 |website=The Lomax Digital Archive |language=en}}</ref> MacColl printed the lyrics and melody in a book of Teesdale folk songs, and later included it on his and [[Peggy Seeger]]'s ''The Singing Island'' in 1960.<ref name=":0" />

==Recordings==
[[File:Scarborough Fair.ogg|thumb|Solo soprano voice]]
===Field recordings===
Early audio field recordings of the ballad include the following examples:
* Georgia Ann Griffin of [[Newberry, Florida|Newberry]], [[Alachua County, Florida|Alachua]], [[Florida]]. Recorded by [[John Lomax]] in 1939.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Cambric Shirt (Roud Folksong Index S230643)|url=https://www.vwml.org/record/RoudFS/S230643|access-date=2020-08-29|website=[[Vaughan Williams Memorial Library]]}}</ref>
* Allie Long Parker of Hogscald Hollow, [[Eureka Springs, Arkansas|Eureka Springs]], [[Arkansas]]. Recorded by [[Mary Parler]] on 7 April 1958.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Rosemary and Thyme (child No. 2) (Roud Folksong Index S407682)|url=https://www.vwml.org/record/RoudFS/S407682|access-date=2020-08-29|website=[[Vaughan Williams Memorial Library]]}}</ref>
* Sara Cleveland of [[Brant Lake, New York|Brant Lake]], [[New York (state)|New York]]. Recorded by [[Sandy Paton]] in 1966.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Every Rose Grows Merry in Time (Roud Folksong Index S204527)|url=https://www.vwml.org/record/RoudFS/S204527|access-date=2020-08-29|website=[[Vaughan Williams Memorial Library]]}}</ref>
* Elizabeth "Liz" Jefferies. Recorded in [[Bristol]] by Barry and Chris Morgan in 1976.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Rosemary Lane (Roud Folksong Index S189118)|url=https://www.vwml.org/record/RoudFS/S189118|access-date=2020-08-29|website=[[Vaughan Williams Memorial Library]]}}</ref>

===Commercial recordings===

====1950s====
The earliest commercial recording of the ballad was made by actors and singers [[Gordon Heath]] and [[Lee Payant]], Americans who ran a café and nightclub, L'Abbaye, on the [[Rive Gauche]] in Paris. The recording appeared on the 1955 [[Elektra Records|Elektra]] album ''Encores from the Abbaye''.<ref>{{AllMusic|last=Heath|first=Gordon|title=''Encores from the Abbaye''|class=album|id=mw0001446411}}</ref> The song was also included on the 1956 album ''The English and Scottish Popular Ballads vol IV'' by [[A. L. Lloyd]] and [[Ewan MacColl]], using Kidson's melody.<ref>{{cite web |last1=LLoyd |first1=A.L. |title=Ewan MacColl's Discography |url=http://ewan-maccoll.info/AlbumInfo.aspx?ID=105 |website=ewan-maccoll.Info |access-date=9 October 2022}}</ref>

The first recorded version using the best-known melody was performed by Audrey Coppard on the 1956 album ''English Folk Songs''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Scarborough Fair|url=https://folkways.si.edu/audrey-coppard/scarborough-fair/celtic-world/music/track/smithsonian|access-date=2020-08-29|website=Smithsonian Folkways Recordings|language=en-US}}</ref> A decade after collecting the song, MacColl released his own version, accompanied by [[Peggy Seeger]] on guitar, on the 1957 LP ''Matching Songs of the British Isles and America''<ref>{{Cite web|title=Matching Songs of the British Isles and America : Ewan MacColl at theBalladeers|url=https://www.theballadeers.com/eng/ewm_1957_rlp637_matching.htm|access-date=2020-10-31|website=www.theballadeers.com|archive-date=16 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201116104029/https://www.theballadeers.com/eng/ewm_1957_rlp637_matching.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> and an [[A cappella|a capella]] rendition another decade later on the 10-CD collection ''The Long Harvest'' (1967).<ref>{{Cite web|title=''The Long Harvest'' traditional English and Scottish ballads sung by Peggy Seeger and Ewan MacColl|type=track listing|url=https://www.peggyseeger.com/listen-buy/the-long-harvest/the-long-harvest|access-date=2025-12-04|website=peggyseeger.com}}</ref>

[[Milt Okun]] and [[Ellen Stekert]] recorded the song as "The Cambric Shirt" on their 1957 album ''Traditional American Love Songs''.<ref>{{AllMusic|title=''Traditional American Love Songs'' – Milton Okun|class=album|id=mw0001494021|last=Eder|first=Bruce}}</ref> David Dicaire, in his 2011 book ''The Folk Music Revival. Biographies Of Fifty Performers And Other Influential People'', called Stekert and Okun's version a "folk classic".<ref name="Dicaire2011">{{cite book |last= Dicaire |first= David |author-link= |date=2011 |title= The Folk Music Revival. Biographies Of Fifty Performers And Other Influential People |url= https://archive.org/details/folkmusicrevival0000dica/ |location= Jefferson, North Carolina |publisher= McFarland & Co. |page=17 |isbn= 9780786463527 |access-date=2025-06-25}}</ref>

====1960s====
In 1965, [[Martin Carthy]] sang "Scarborough Fair" on his [[Martin Carthy (album)|eponymous debut album]] after having picked up the tune from the songbook by MacColl and Seeger.<ref name=Humphries>{{Cite web|last=Humphries|first=Patrick|date=2003|work=Sold on Song|title=Scarborough Fair, Martin Carthy|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/radio2/soldonsong/songlibrary/indepth/scarborough.shtml|access-date=2025-12-04|publisher=[[BBC]]}}</ref>

[[Marianne Faithfull]] recorded the song for her second American studio album ''[[Go Away from My World]]'', released in December 1965.

"Scarborough Fair/Canticle" appeared as the lead track on the 1966 [[Simon & Garfunkel]] album ''[[Parsley, Sage, Rosemary and Thyme]]'' in [[counterpoint]] with "Canticle", a reworking of the lyrics from Simon's 1963 [[anti-war]] song "The Side of a Hill".<ref name="song_and_lyrics">{{cite web |url=http://www.paulsimon.com/song/scarborough-faircanticle/ |title=Song and Lyrics, Scarborough Fair/Canticle |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |website=PaulSimon.com |publisher=[[Sony Music]] |access-date=10 July 2016}}</ref> The duo learned their arrangement of the song from Martin Carthy, but did not credit him as the arranger<ref name="acroutes">{{cite AV media |people=Jan Leman|date= 1992|title= Acoustic routes|language=en}} See at 46 min.</ref>. They later made a "pretty substantial" monetary settlement with Carthy's publisher when asked, but unbeknownst to them, Carthy himself did not receive anything from it.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-03-01 |title=The story behind Simon & Garfunkel's song 'Scarborough Fair' |url=https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/the-story-behind-simon-garfunkel-song-scarborough-fair/ |access-date=2024-11-11 |website=faroutmagazine.co.uk |language=en-US}}</ref>

[[Sérgio Mendes]] and Brasil '66 scored a U.S. No. 16 hit (#2 AC) with their light jazz/samba/pop version in 1968, which was used in the 1973 animated film ''[[Heavy Traffic]]''.{{Citation needed|date=December 2024}}

In 1969, [[Vicky Leandros]] recorded the song in several versions for release throughout Europe, Canada and Japan, singing in English, German, French ("Chèvrefeuille que tu es loin") and Greek ("Νά Θυμάσαι Πώς Μ' αγαπάς").{{citation needed|date=October 2021}}

Dutch [[progressive rock]] band [[Brainbox (band)|Brainbox]] recorded a version of the song on their 1969 album ''Brainbox''.

The song is the last track featured in [[Bobbie Gentry]]'s and [[Glen Campbell]]'s 1968 collaborative album ''[[Bobbie Gentry and Glen Campbell]]''.

====1980s====
American [[folk punk]] band [[Cordelia's Dad]] recorded a version for their 1989 self-titled debut album.<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Cordelia's Dad'', by Cordelia's Dad |url=https://cordeliasdad.bandcamp.com/album/cordelias-dad |access-date=2024-07-14 |website=CordeliasDad.bandcamp.com|language=en}}</ref>

[[The Stone Roses]] set their own words to the melody for "Elizabeth My Dear", a track on their [[The Stone Roses (album)|eponymous debut album]] (1989).{{Citation needed|date=December 2024}}

Philadelphia punk band Tons of Nuns recorded the song on their second demo and performed the song live on WXPN.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tons of Nuns – Freedom Has No Bounds |url=https://freedomhasnobounds.com/category/philly-bands/tons-of-nuns/ |access-date=2025-10-05 |language=en-US}}</ref>

====1990s====
[[Queensrÿche]] included a version as the B-side of their single "Anybody Listening?" in 1992.<ref name="Honigmann 2020">{{cite web |last=Honigmann |first=David |title=Scarborough Fair — the ancient ballad that sparked a modern-day grudge |website=FT.com |date=August 9, 2020 |url=https://subs.ft.com/products?location=https%3A%2F%2F%2Flife-of-a-song%2Fscarborough-fair.html |access-date=2023-11-23}}</ref> It was later included as a bonus track on the 2003 reissue of their album ''[[Empire (Queensrÿche album)|Empire]]''.

====2000s====
[[Celtic Woman]] recorded a version of the song for their third album ''[[A New Journey]]'', released in January 2007.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.celticwoman.com/|title=Celtic Woman Story|first=Granite|last=Digital|website=www.celticwoman.com}}</ref>

English [[early music]] ensemble [[Mediæval Bæbes]] recorded a version entitled "Scarborough Fayre" for their 2005 album ''Mirabilis''.

The English [[death-doom|death-doom metal]] band [[My Dying Bride]] recorded a version with two additional stanzas by its lead singer [[Aaron Stainthorpe]], which appears on its 2009 EP ''[[Bring Me Victory]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.metalunderground.com/news/details.cfm?newsid=47728|work=Metal Underground|title=My Dying Bride Completes Recording New EP, "Bring Me Victory"|access-date=5 January 2025}}</ref>

German/Norwegian [[symphonic metal]] band [[Leaves' Eyes]] recorded a version of this song on their 2009 album ''[[Njord (album)|Njord]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/music/reviews/93mq|work=[[BBC Music]]|title=Leaves' Eyes Njord review|first=Greg|last=Moffitt|year=2009|access-date=5 January 2025}}</ref>

====2010s====

[[Nox Arcana]] recorded a ghost-story version with all original lyrics by Joseph Vargo for the 2012 album ''[[Winter's Majesty]]''.<ref>{{YouTube|title='Scarborough Fair' by Nox Arcana with original lyrics|id=sgbo2QWLBzI}}</ref>

In 2017, [[Aurora (singer)|Aurora]] recorded the song for the Brazilian [[telenovela]] ''[[Deus Salve o Rei]]'' along with an [[opening sequence]] for it.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://gshow.globo.com/novelas/deus-salve-o-rei/noticia/aurora-cantora-norueguesa-grava-clipe-da-musica-de-abertura-de-deus-salve-o-rei-nos-estudios-globo.ghtml |title=Aurora, cantora norueguesa, grava clipe da música de abertura de 'Deus Salve o Rei' nos Estúdios Globo |access-date=22 November 2017 |date=23 October 2017 |website=Gshow |language=pt-BR |archive-date=24 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171024043707/https://gshow.globo.com/novelas/deus-salve-o-rei/noticia/aurora-cantora-norueguesa-grava-clipe-da-musica-de-abertura-de-deus-salve-o-rei-nos-estudios-globo.ghtml |url-status=live}}</ref>

====2020s====
In 2020, [[Dan Avidan]] & Super Guitar Bros released it as part of their first collaborative album.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scarborough Fair|url=https://danavidan.bandcamp.com/track/scarborough-fair |access-date=2026-10-04 |website=danavidan.bandcamp.com}}</ref>

In 2025, [[Oli Steadman]] included it on his song collection "365 Days Of Folk".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://airtable.com/app0wHIAKsGSxDfp8/shrZ0JeqDDGlBmXve|title=365 Days Of Folk: Song List|access-date=24 January 2026}}</ref>

In 2026, [[Dorian Electra]] included it on their self-titled EP of covers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dorian Electra's Instagram |url=https://www.instagram.com/p/DW4NxoSjdkd/ |access-date=2026-04-19 |website=www.instagram.com}}</ref>

In London in 1965, [[Paul Simon]] learned the song from [[Martin Carthy]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/radio2/soldonsong/songlibrary/indepth/scarborough.shtml |title=Sold on Song – Song Library – Scarborough Fair |publisher=[[BBC]] |website=bbc.co.uk/radio2 |language=en |access-date=2017-11-23}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://tabs.ultimate-guitar.com/tab/simon-garfunkel/scarborough-fair-chords-2007315|title=Simon & Garfunkel – Scarborough Fair (Chords)|via=tabs.ultimate-guitar.com}}</ref> who had picked up the song from the songbook by MacColl and Seeger<ref name=Humphries /> and included it on [[Martin Carthy (album)|his eponymous 1965 album]]. [[Simon & Garfunkel]] set it in [[counterpoint]] with "Canticle", a reworking of the lyrics from Simon's 1963 [[anti-war]] song "The Side of a Hill";<ref name="song_and_lyrics" /> they used the tune score provided to Paul Simon by Carthy<ref name="acroutes" />, while Simon's anti-war lyrics were set to a new melody composed mainly by [[Art Garfunkel]].<ref name=Humphries /><ref name="Bennighof2007">{{cite book |last=Bennighof |first=James |title=The Words and Music of Paul Simon |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ShBhKL-9SLIC&pg=PA21 |access-date=19 June 2015 |year=2007 |publisher=[[Greenwood Publishing Group]] |isbn=9780275991630 |pages=21–24}}</ref> "Scarborough Fair/Canticle" appeared as the lead track on the 1966 album ''[[Parsley, Sage, Rosemary and Thyme]]'', and was released as a single after it had been featured on [[The Graduate (soundtrack)|the soundtrack]] to ''[[The Graduate]]'' in 1968.<ref name=Humphries /> The [[copyright]] credited only Simon and Garfunkel as the authors, which upset Carthy, who felt that the "traditional" source should have been [[credit (creative arts)|credited]].<ref name=Humphries /> The rift persisted until Simon invited Carthy to perform the song with him as a duet in a concert at London's [[Hammersmith Apollo]] in October 2000.<ref name=Humphries /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.setlist.fm/setlist/paul-simon/2000/hammersmith-apollo-london-england-33c83495.html|title=Paul Simon Setlist at Hammersmith Apollo, London|website=setlist.fm}}</ref> Simon performed the song with [[the Muppets]] when he guest-starred on season 5, episode 11 of ''[[The Muppet Show]]'' (October 18, 1980).

Before Simon learned the song, [[Bob Dylan]] had borrowed the melody and several lines of lyrics from Carthy's arrangement to create his song "[[Girl from the North Country]]",<ref>{{Cite web |url= http://www.justanothertune.com/html/gotnc.html |title= "...She Once Was A True Love of Mine" – Some Notes About Bob Dylan's "Girl From The North Country" |author=Jürgen Kloss|website=justanothertune.com |access-date= 2017-11-23}}</ref> which is featured on ''[[The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan]]'' (1963), ''[[Nashville Skyline]]'' (1969) (with [[Johnny Cash]]), ''[[Real Live]]'' (1984) and ''[[The 30th Anniversary Concert Celebration]]'' (1993).

=== Soundtrack recordings ===

The Simon and Garfunkel version of the song was featured on [[The Graduate (soundtrack)|the soundtrack]] to ''[[The Graduate]]'' in 1968.<ref name=Humphries />

Instrumental versions of "Scarborough Fair" were arranged by [[Geoff Knorr]] for use in the video game ''[[Civilization VI]]'' as the main theme of the English civilization.<ref>{{YouTube|title=England Theme – Industrial (''Civilization 6'' OST) {{!}} Scarborough Fair|id=NG_AZky2Xkc}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2016-07-22 |title=''Civilization VI'' to feature an orchestral soundtrack led by Knorr and Tin |url=http://www.vgmonline.net/civilization-vi-to-feature-an-orchestral-soundtrack-led-by-knorr-and-tin/ |access-date=2022-08-04 |website=VGMO – Video Game Music Online}}</ref> As the themes of each civilization are played as different variations of the same song as the game progresses, four different variations of the song are included in the [[Music of the Civilization series|game's soundtrack]], with Phill Boucher assisting Knorr in the arrangement of the [[Atomic Era]] version of the song.<ref>{{Cite news |author=Tom Marks |date=2016-09-30 |title=''Civ 6''{{'}}s music evolves alongside your cities, and it's one of its best features|work=[[PC Gamer]]|url=https://www.pcgamer.com/how-civilization-6s-music-evolves-through-the-eras/ |access-date=2022-08-04}}</ref><ref>{{YouTube|title=''Civilization VI'' Official Game Soundtrack|id=eqJFVg05b8Q}}</ref>
